mcqs.question: When reconciliation compares an old `<EditForm/>` node to a new `<ViewForm/>` node at the same position, what happens?
options: The differing props are patched onto the existing instance
React defers the decision until the next render
The two are merged into a single component instance
The old instance is unmounted and a new one is mounted, because they are different types
mcqs.explanation: The same-type-vs-different-type heuristic runs before anything else is compared — different component types are never considered for in-place reuse, so the old instance (and any state it held) is torn down and a fresh one is created, no matter how similar the two render.

mcqs.question: Without a `key`, how does reconciliation match old list items to new list items?
options: By comparing items at the same index position
By comparing the deep equality of each item's full contents
By checking each item's memory reference from the previous render
By re-fetching the list's data source and diffing it server-side
mcqs.explanation: With no key, position is the only signal the algorithm has, so it pairs old index 0 with new index 0 and so on — correct when a list only grows or shrinks at the end, wrong the moment items are inserted at the front or reordered.

mcqs.question: A list uses `key={index}`. What happens to a row's internal state after an item is deleted from the middle of the list?
options: All internal state across every row is reset to its initial value
State can end up attached to the wrong row, because every row after the deletion shifts to an index that used to belong to a different item
The framework detects the deletion and preserves state correctly regardless of key choice
The component throws a runtime error requiring a page reload
mcqs.explanation: Deleting an item shifts every following item's index down by one, so the framework matches the component instance previously at that index — state included — to whatever data now occupies it, which is a different item. It doesn't reset everything or error; it silently mismatches.

mcqs.question: What do Vue's compiler-generated "patch flags" let the reconciler skip?
options: Mounting components that are conditionally rendered
Calling any lifecycle hooks during an update
Diffing static parts of a template that the compiler already knows can never change
Creating a virtual DOM tree entirely
mcqs.explanation: The template compiler marks which nodes are ever dynamic ahead of time, so the runtime diff can skip static subtrees entirely instead of comparing them and finding no difference every time. Vue still builds and diffs a virtual DOM — patch flags narrow that work, they don't remove it.

mcqs.question: Why does React's reconciliation run in O(n) instead of the O(n³) a general tree-diff algorithm would require?
options: Because it only ever compares trees of exactly the same depth
Because it skips reconciliation entirely for lists under a certain size
Because the virtual DOM is smaller than the real DOM by a constant factor
Because it assumes different element types produce substantially different trees and trusts `key` for identity, avoiding a general search for the best match
mcqs.explanation: The heuristics trade generality for speed: type mismatches are resolved by replacing rather than searching for a partial match, and `key` gives identity directly instead of requiring the algorithm to infer the best possible item correspondence, which is the expensive part of a general tree diff.
